sections.heading: Trusting what you have shown us in your Word
sections.text: God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, we put our hope in what you have said. In your Word, you do not show yourself to us only as the Judge we should fear, but as the God who welcomes sinners to come for mercy. You sit on a throne of grace, ready to be kind, and you call people like us to look to you and be saved, because there is no other God besides you. Help us to know your name truly, and because we know you, to trust you.
theological_themes: God reveals himself in Scripture as holy Judge and merciful Savior.
Sinners are invited to come to God for saving grace rather than flee from him in despair.
True knowledge of God leads to trust.

scripture_references.connection: This passage invites believers to draw near to God’s throne for mercy and grace because Jesus, the great high priest, has opened the way. It supports the prayer’s confidence that God receives needy sinners rather than merely condemning them.
God declares that he alone is God and Savior and calls the ends of the earth to turn to him for salvation. This grounds the prayer’s hope in God’s own saving invitation.
The psalm connects knowing God’s name with trusting him, because God does not abandon those who seek him. That is the movement of this section: from God’s revealed character to confident dependence.

sections.heading: Giving you all the credit for saving sinners
sections.text: Father, heaven is full of people who are living proof of your mercy, and even now on earth there are countless witnesses to your grace. You have rescued ruined people from the wreckage sin has made of us. Every person who has ever been saved has been saved by you, not by their own goodness, strength, or wisdom. So we join their song: the glory belongs to you, not to us, because your mercy and faithfulness have done it all.
theological_themes: Salvation is entirely the work of God’s free and effective grace.
The rescue of sinners displays the riches of God’s mercy.
God alone deserves the glory for salvation.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes sinners as spiritually dead and then shows God making them alive by grace through faith, not as a result of works. This directly supports the prayer’s claim that recovery from the Fall is God’s doing and not our achievement.
The psalm gives glory to God’s name because of his steadfast love and faithfulness. It captures the prayer’s refusal to take credit for salvation and its desire to praise God alone.

sections.heading: Coming to you through Jesus, our Mediator
sections.text: You have chosen to deal with us through Jesus Christ, the one Mediator you have given. Everything we need is found in him. He is full of grace and truth, exalted as our Prince and Savior. We look to him, we lean on him, and through him we are made right with you. Keep us from trusting any other foundation—our feelings, our obedience, our reputation, or our efforts. Let Christ be enough for us.
theological_themes: God relates savingly to sinners through the one Mediator, Jesus Christ.
The fullness needed for salvation is found in Christ.
Justification comes through Christ, not through human merit.

scripture_references.connection: This passage names Christ Jesus as the one Mediator between God and humanity, who gave himself as a ransom. It directly grounds the prayer’s approach to God through Christ alone.
Paul teaches that all fullness dwells in Christ and that God reconciles through him. This supports the prayer’s confidence that everything needed for peace with God is found in Jesus.
Peter speaks of Jesus as exalted by God as Leader and Savior, giving repentance and forgiveness. This matches the prayer’s confession of Christ as the exalted Prince and Savior.
Paul explains that sinners are justified by God’s grace through the redemption in Christ Jesus. This grounds the prayer’s statement that we are made right with God through Christ.

sections.heading: Receiving the comfort of the cross without making peace with sin
sections.text: Lord Jesus, let your suffering bring real relief to our troubled hearts, but never let us become casual about the sin that made your suffering necessary. Let your blood quiet our consciences and cleanse us from guilt. Make us deeply thankful for your sacrifice, and also glad to belong to you and serve you. Let your love take hold of us so that we stop living as if our lives are our own, and instead live for you.
theological_themes: Christ’s atoning death gives comfort to guilty consciences.
The cross both assures pardon and deepens hatred of sin.
Christ’s love moves believers away from self-centered living into devoted service.

scripture_references.connection: The passage says Christ’s blood purifies the conscience and enables service to the living God. It supports the prayer’s double emphasis on inward peace and renewed obedience.
John connects fellowship with God, cleansing by Jesus’ blood, honest confession, and forgiveness. This fits the prayer’s desire for cleansing without minimizing sin.

Paul says Christ’s love controls believers because Christ died so that they would no longer live for themselves but for him. This directly supports the prayer’s request to be constrained by Christ’s love.

sections.heading: Learning gratitude instead of complaint
sections.text: Father, give us grateful and steady hearts. When our wishes are not granted, keep us from complaining. When our joys come mixed with trials, keep us from acting as though you have treated us badly. We know what we deserve apart from your mercy, and we also know how many and how great your gifts to us have been. Teach us to bless you and praise you at all times.
theological_themes: Gratitude grows from remembering both our undeserving state and God’s many benefits.
Believers are called to resist murmuring even when desires are denied or trials accompany joys.
Praise is fitting in every circumstance because God’s mercy is greater than our complaints.

scripture_references.connection: Paul calls believers to rejoice, pray, and give thanks in all circumstances as God’s will in Christ. This supports the prayer’s desire for gratitude even when life is not arranged according to our wishes.
Paul warns against grumbling and urges believers to live as lights in the world. This connects with the prayer’s request to be kept from murmuring and repining.
The psalm summons the soul to bless the Lord and remember his benefits. It supports the prayer’s final movement from awareness of mercy to continual praise.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original strongly emphasizes human ruin from the Fall and complete dependence on grace; this is historically Reformed and broadly Protestant, but the phrasing can be doctrinally contested by traditions with a different account of original sin and human ability.

The phrase about deriving relief from Christ’s sufferings while still abhorring sin needed careful handling so the adaptation would not imply that the atonement makes sin less serious or that assurance weakens holiness.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Thou hast chosen to transact all thy concerns with us through a Mediator” was rendered as God choosing to deal savingly with us through Jesus Christ, because the context centers on salvation, justification, and access to God rather than every possible act of providence.

“The double efficacy of his blood, tranquillizing and cleansing our consciences” was expressed as quieting troubled consciences and cleansing from guilt, preserving both the assurance/peace and purification themes without using technical or archaic language.
“Sensible of our desert” was rendered as remembering what we deserve apart from mercy, because the original uses human unworthiness to deepen gratitude rather than to produce despair.
